record.paper_title: Ramsey theory of homogeneous structures: current trends and open problems
record.original_question: For big Ramsey degree results whose known proofs use forcing, find purely combinatorial proofs. The problem is especially open for k-clique-free homogeneous graphs with k at least 4 and for other relevant free-amalgamation-property classes, where the free amalgamation property is strong amalgamation with no additional relations beyond those inherited from the two structures being amalgamated.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A class K of finite structures in a fixed relational language is said to have the strong amalgamation property (SAP) if for any A, B, C in K with embeddings f: A → B and g: A → C, there exist D in K and embeddings r: B → D and s: C → D such that r∘f = s∘g and r(B) ∩ s(C) = r(f(A)) = s(g(A)). The class K has the free amalgamation property (FAP) if it has the SAP and, moreover, D can always be chosen so that no relations hold in D except those inherited from B (via r) and C (via s).

Given a Fraïssé limit M of such a class K, and a finite substructure A of M, the big Ramsey degree T(A, M) is the least integer T (if it exists) such that for every finite coloring of the copies of A in M, there is a copy M' of M inside M whose copies of A take at most T colors.

Several known results establish finite big Ramsey degrees for Fraïssé limits of FAP classes (including the universal homogeneous k-clique-free graph for various k) by proofs that use the method of set-theoretic forcing, applied to auxiliary "coding tree" structures.

Problem. For each big Ramsey degree result whose only currently known proof uses the method of forcing, produce a purely combinatorial proof of the same result, that is, a proof which does not invoke forcing arguments. Address in particular the following cases:

(i) The k-clique-free homogeneous (Henson) graph H_k for every integer k ≥ 4: give a purely combinatorial proof that every finite k-clique-free graph A has a finite big Ramsey degree in H_k.

(ii) Fraïssé limits of other FAP classes (in arbitrary finite relational languages) for which finiteness of big Ramsey degrees is currently established only via forcing-based methods on coding trees: provide purely combinatorial proofs of finiteness and, where possible, of the exact values of the big Ramsey degrees.
artifact.category_tag: Big Ramsey degrees of homogeneous structures
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2022–2026) has produced combinatorial frameworks (e.g., Balko–Chodounský–Dobrinen–Hubička–Konečný–Vena–Zucker on binary free amalgamation classes, and a 2025 preprint counting big Ramsey degrees of the K_4-free Henson graph) that reprove or extend several big Ramsey degree results without forcing. However, the original proofs of finiteness of big Ramsey degrees for the Henson graphs H_k via Dobrinen's strong coding trees rely essentially on forcing, and no fully combinatorial replacement has been published for all FAP classes; the problem of eliminating forcing in these proofs remains an active open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Counting big Ramsey degrees of the homogeneous and universal K_4-free graph
status_evidence.snippet: Computes big Ramsey degrees of small graphs in the K_4-free Henson graph using combinatorial methods on coding trees.
status_evidence.claim: Recent combinatorial advances exist for the K_4-free case, but general FAP classes are not fully covered.

status_evidence.title: On big Ramsey degrees for binary free amalgamation classes
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizes big Ramsey degrees of Fraïssé limits of finitely constrained free amalgamation classes in finite binary languages.
status_evidence.claim: Combinatorial characterizations have been obtained in the binary FAP setting, partially addressing the request.

status_evidence.title: The Ramsey theory of Henson graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Proves finiteness of big Ramsey degrees for k-clique-free Henson graphs using strong coding trees and forcing arguments.
status_evidence.claim: The original proofs for k-clique-free Henson graphs use forcing, motivating the search for combinatorial replacements.
